Sargo-class submarine USS Saury underway off Mare Island Navy Yard, Vallejo, California, United States, 28 May 1944. Note that Saury’s deck gun has been moved back to abaft the conning tower.

USS Saury (SS 189) was launched on August 20, 1938 at the Electric Boat Company in Groton, Connecticut, and commissioned on April 3, 1939. A Sargo-class fleet submarine built for long-range Pacific operations, she was stationed in the Philippines as part of the Asiatic Fleet when war erupted in December 1941, placing her squarely in the path of Japan's opening offensive.

When the attack came, Saury was based at Manila, and her first war patrol took her into the South China Sea to hunt along the Indochina coast. Like nearly every American submarine in those early months, she was crippled by the notoriously defective Mark 14 torpedo, which routinely ran too deep, failed to detonate, or circled erratically. As the Philippines fell, she withdrew through the Dutch East Indies, operating briefly out of Surabaya before relocating to Fremantle, Australia. Her second patrol in early 1942 brought her against a Japanese convoy off Borneo, and although she is credited with damaging enemy shipping, the persistent torpedo failures kept confirmed sinkings stubbornly low.

As the war progressed, Saury shifted her base to Pearl Harbor and ranged across the Central Pacific and East China Sea, pressing attacks on Japanese merchant traffic and warships through 1942 and into 1943. One of her most notable engagements came when she ambushed a Japanese light cruiser and scored hits that inflicted damage, though the cruiser managed to escape. She sank the merchantman Kanan Maru and damaged additional enemy tonnage across her successive patrols, often working some of the most heavily contested waters of the Pacific, including the approaches to the Japanese home islands.

By 1944, Saury was an aging boat compared to the newer Gato and Balao class submarines flooding into the fleet, and after completing twelve war patrols she was withdrawn from frontline service and reassigned to training duty on the U.S. East Coast, where she helped prepare fresh submarine crews at New London, Connecticut. She was decommissioned on October 22, 1945, just weeks after Japan's surrender, and was later expended as a target before being sold for scrap in 1947. For her wartime service she received seven battle stars, a record that reflected both the breadth of her patrols and the hard, often thankless work she carried out across nearly four years of Pacific war.
